summary:
British Columbia stands under the Canadian framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation and hate-propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code, both carried by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia, and sexual orientation has been covered federally since 1996. Courts have applied these protections consistently.

British Columbia has no hostile provincial legislation. It was the first jurisdiction in Canada to write sexual orientation into its human-rights code, in 1992, and it is routinely assessed as the country's most progressive province on LGBT issues; Vancouver's Davie Village remains the established social centre. No province or territory restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Legal gender recognition operates on a self-declaration basis. Transgender people may change their legal gender in every province and territory, British Columbia included, under rules that vary from place to place; Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act replaced the surgery requirement with a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. Federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

A 2021 amendment to the Criminal Code, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide, for minors and for adults. Coverage of health care is universal.

The visible risk to a visitor is the hate-crime climate rather than the statute book. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in Canada in 2024, up 1% on 2023 after a 34% rise the year before; the total is up 169% since 2018, a more than doubling, while the population rate fell 2% to 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, and religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. Offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression remain among the fastest-growing categories over the longer arc, and Egale Canada publishes an analysis of the 2024 data affecting 2SLGBTQI people. The national figures carry no British Columbia breakdown.

Hostility is also visible in British Columbia itself. In 2023, coordinated disruptions repeatedly targeted public drag-storytime events at libraries: Coquitlam Public Library postponed or cancelled on several occasions, including a protest at its Town Centre branch on 14 January 2023 and a postponement on 13 October 2023, citing public-safety risk, while the counter-gathering that followed became the largest queer gathering the Tri-Cities had seen. At a Richmond library event with no police on site, a man pushed through the crowd to photograph attendees.

Detention is the weakest part of the national framework. Since Bill C-16, federal correctional policy requires transgender prisoners to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Both placement and gender-affirming treatment have been contested in court, including litigation in which lawyer Barbara findlay represented a trans prisoner challenging placement in a women's institution and the withholding of gender-affirming medical care.

Two provinces have moved against residents. Alberta and Saskatchewan have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans people living there, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. These rules govern residents rather than visitors, but they mark the direction of provincial politics running alongside the human-rights statutes.
tangentialFactors:
The national baseline equality score of 0.86 rests on Charter equality protection, nationwide conversion-therapy criminalisation, and legal gender change available in every province, British Columbia included.

The 2024 statistics describe a mixed picture rather than a single trend. The overall count of police-reported hate crime rose again while the rate per 100,000 residents fell, and sexual-orientation-motivated incidents dropped after three consecutive annual increases from a 2023 peak of 889. Across six consecutive years police-reported hate crime is up 169% since 2018, and Egale Canada documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement.

The Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 covers Canada as a whole. A visitor assessing British Columbia has to reason from national data plus documented provincial incidents, since no province-level hate-crime figures appear in the source set.

British Columbia's position contrasts with the two provinces that have legislated rollbacks and with provinces that still attach conditions to document changes. None of those measures binds a visitor in British Columbia.
localsOnly:
British Columbia's human-rights code has covered sexual orientation since 1992 and discrimination complaints have a defined route, with the provincial human-rights process handling claims that include gender identity and gender expression.

Residents are covered by universal provincial health-care coverage, and legal gender change on official documents is available locally under the province's declaration process.

School-facing rules on names, pronouns and parental notification adopted in Alberta and Saskatchewan do not apply to British Columbia schools; the province has no equivalent statute.

Community institutions in the province absorbed sustained protest pressure through 2023, and the response at Coquitlam and Richmond libraries included counter-gatherings organised by local residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Statistics Canada figures of 30 March 2026 are national and contain no British Columbia breakdown, so province-specific hate-crime counts for 2024 are unresolved in this record.

The existence of Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis is sourced; its province-level findings are not summarised here and remain unverified.

No source in the inventory documents conversion-therapy prosecutions, complaint outcomes, or hate-crime prosecutions in British Columbia specifically; enforcement in the province is therefore not established either way.

No entry-, visa-, or border-screening incident data for trans travellers to Canada appears in the inventory beyond the statement that no alerts have been issued or received.
